name: Xin26x
baseline: x265 (--preset fast, single thread, build dated 2020-12-25)
workload: Single-thread low-delay IPPP encode of four clips (1080p BasketballDrive, 1080p pedestrian_area, 720p KristenAndSara, 1080p sc_desktop screen content) at matched bitrate, frames per second and PSNR; separate offline table gives BD-rate against x265 veryslow.
claimed_speedup: FPS xin26x vs x265: BasketballDrive 20.68 vs 7.96 (PSNR 36.929 vs 36.913); pedestrian_area 39.203 vs 8.35 (39.719 vs 39.707); KristenAndSara 103.68 vs 23.56 (43.218 vs 43.183); sc_desktop 39.48 vs 16.83 (40.082 vs 29.817). README text: 'The performance of xin26x(HEVC) is x4 compared to x265 under single unit core.' Ratios 2.6x, 4.7x, 4.4x, 2.3x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Build via CMake and Visual Studio 2022 (README); optimization flags not stated; a prebuilt win64 exe is shipped in testbin. x265 command lines are listed in the README (--preset fast --pools 1 --bframes 0 --frame-threads 0 --no-wpp --tune psnr); xin26x lines use --thread 1 --wpp 0 --bframes 0 with --preset 0 or 3.
tradeoffs: Requires x86 with AVX2 (README lists no other CPU support). Build scripts target Windows (CMake plus Visual Studio). HEVC and VVC encoders only; AV1 is intra-only pure C without SIMD or threads. Max resolution stated as 3860x2160, max 3 temporal layers, evaluation mode supports ABR only. AGPL-3.0 copyleft. Plain C API.
caveats: First-party numbers; the README states no CPU model, so tier C. x265 is an old build (2020-12-25) at preset fast, while xin26x runs its own presets 0 and 3, so the pairing is not preset-matched. PSNR is near-equal on three clips, but on the screen-content clip x265 scores 29.817 dB vs 40.082 dB because x265 ran without screen-content tools, so that row is not a fair speed comparison. README says lookahead and cu-tree were enabled on both and that a real RTC encoder would be faster. The offline BD-rate table (x265 veryslow reference) has no timing. Repository history starts 2026-04-28, so the project is new. Bitstreams are on Google Drive, not in the repo.
found_via: Blogs / talks pass: the WebSearch queries on H.264/HEVC encoders surfaced no hit; the project came from the github.com/topics/vvc listing ('Video Encoder for Now and Next Decade'); README read via raw.githubusercontent.com and the repo page opened with WebFetch.

name: Nelux (NeLux)
language: C++ (Python package with PyTorch tensor output)
baseline: FFmpeg CLI piped decode (ffmpeg-rgb24 subprocess; ffmpeg-nvdec subprocess for the GPU path); torchcodec also compared
workload: H.264 decode to RGB uint8 HWC tensors at 720p, 1080p and 4K, 600 frames per run (300 at 4K), median of 5 fresh subprocess runs; CPU path and NVDEC path.
claimed_speedup: CPU, fps nelux default vs ffmpeg-rgb24 vs torchcodec: 720p 3422 vs 2273 vs 2924; 1080p 2642 vs 1102 vs 1589; 4K 607 vs 254 vs 367. NVDEC fps nelux vs ffmpeg-nvdec: 720p 1651 vs 1253; 1080p 667 vs 592; 4K 175 vs 162 (README: 8-32% faster at lower CPU).
compiler_and_flags: Compiler and flags not stated. FFmpeg 8.x (bundled TAS-FFMPEG 8.1.2), PyTorch 2.11+cu130, nelux 0.11.0, Windows 11. README gives reproduction commands: python tests/comprehensive_bench.py --tag mybox and python tests/bench_thread_modes.py.
tradeoffs: About 2.5-3x the CPU use of torchcodec in default mode (convert worker pool); needs PyTorch imported first; AGPL-3.0, and the bundled FFmpeg binaries are GPL-2.0-or-later (libx264 and libx265 linked in). Python API over a C++ core.
caveats: The README itself says the win over torchcodec is entirely the convert worker pool: with convert_workers=0 nelux is within about 2% of torchcodec (720p 3167 vs 3090, 1080p 1755 vs 1728, 4K 394 vs 401). The ffmpeg baseline is a subprocess pipe including process and pipe overhead, so it is not an in-process libavcodec comparison. Figures were last re-measured on 0.11.0 and the decode path has changed since (0.16.0, 0.17.0). Single hardware data point, no flags. Gain over FFmpeg comes mostly from fanning libswscale conversion across cores.
found_via: WebSearch 'torchcodec OR decord OR PyAV video decoding benchmark faster than OpenCV ffmpeg GitHub C++' surfaced NevermindNilas/python-decoders-benchmarks, whose README lists Nelux; repo README read via raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: video_reader-rs
workload: Decode a whole video of shape (2004, 1472, 1472, 3) into a numpy array on a 12-core laptop with 15 GB RAM under Ubuntu 22.04; options are compression factor f, resize of shorter side r, grayscale g.
claimed_speedup: Seconds, OpenCV / decord / vr.decode / vr.decode_fast: f 1.0 65 / 18 / 9.3 / 6.2; f 0.5 33.96 / 14.6 / 5.5 / 4.2; f 0.25 7.16 / 14.03 / 4.2 / 3.8; f 0.25 r 512 6.5 / 13.3 / 3.92 / 3.5; f 0.25 g 20.2 / 25.7 / 6.6 / N/A. README: 'performing equally or better than decord, while using less memory.'
hardware: Laptop with 12-core Intel i7-9750H @ 2.60GHz, 15 GB RAM, Ubuntu 22.04; decord was run on a different machine with more RAM and cores
tradeoffs: Python module built from Rust with FFmpeg bindings, not a C or C++ library; decodes only the requested segments, supports resize during decode, CUDA and VAAPI paths, custom FFmpeg filter chains. Only part of decord's API is implemented.
caveats: First-party table with no compiler or flags and no benchmark script located in the repo root listing. The decord column came from a different, larger machine because decord crashed on the 15 GB laptop, so that column is not like for like. Baselines are OpenCV and decord, not the FFmpeg tools. Speedups depend on the compression-factor and resize options chosen.
found_via: WebSearch 'torchcodec OR decord OR PyAV video decoding benchmark faster than OpenCV ffmpeg GitHub C++' led to python-decoders-benchmarks, whose README lists Video-Reader-RS; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: loudness (iver56)
baseline: pyebur128 (Cython wrapper of libebur128), pyloudnorm, torchaudio, pyloudness
workload: Integrated loudness (LUFS) calculation from audio held as NumPy arrays on CPU; clip length and content not stated.
claimed_speedup: Execution time: loudness 0.1.0 0.056 s; pyebur128 0.1.1 0.096 s; torchaudio 2.8.0 0.282 s; pyloudnorm 0.1.1 0.293 s; pyloudness 1.1.2 0.581 s. README: 'significantly faster than the alternatives when running on CPU'. About 1.7x over pyebur128 (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: C++ core based on Nomono's libloudness (not libebur128) with Python bindings; follows ITU BS.1770 gating; Python-first API, so use from C++ means vendoring the core.
caveats: The numbers appear only in the chart image caption (alt text) of the README; no audio duration, CPU, compiler flags or benchmark script is given. The closest baseline, pyebur128 (a libebur128 wrapper), is only about 1.7x slower; the larger ratios are against pure-Python or torch implementations.
found_via: WebSearch 'EBU R128 loudness meter library faster than libebur128 OR ffmpeg ebur128 benchmark SIMD' snippet ('world's fastest Python package for calculating integrated loudness'); README read via raw.githubusercontent.com and repo page opened.

name: libsonare
workload: Per-feature timing from raw audio on a 73 s synthetic stereo 44.1 kHz fixture resampled to 22.05 kHz, 3 runs per case; plus a full analyze() pipeline versus the librosa-based bpm-detector 1.1.0 --comprehensive.
claimed_speedup: ms librosa vs libsonare: STFT 12.63 vs 6.81 (1.85x); Mel 19.89 vs 15.87 (1.25x); HPSS 1715.77 vs 64.41 (26.64x); Chroma 42.9 vs 8.46 (5.07x); pYIN 5745.04 vs 364.38 (15.77x); MFCC 21.29 vs 16.91 (1.26x); onset strength 20.98 vs 16.76 (1.25x); spectral centroid 24.67 vs 12.1 (2.04x); beat tracking 34.69 vs 44.44 (0.78x, slower). Full analyze 541.45 ms vs bpm-detector 38949.54 ms (71.94x).
compiler_and_flags: Reproduction steps in benchmarks/README.md use cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_BENCH=ON; compiler and extra flags not stated
hardware: 18 hardware threads; CPU model not stated; load average 2.49 before and 3.09 after the run
tradeoffs: Dependency-free C++ core with Python, Node.js and WASM bindings; defaults match librosa where features overlap and CI checks against librosa reference values. Threaded paths use all cores.
caveats: Authors' own benchmark: public scripts but no CPU model, so tier C. Baseline is a Python library (interpreter overhead), and the threaded libsonare paths use many cores. The 71.94x full-pipeline figure compares against a different program (bpm-detector built on librosa), not librosa itself. Beat tracking is slower than librosa. Synthetic fixture only. Audio analysis, not a codec, so fit with the FFmpeg/x264/Opus baseline list is weak.
found_via: github.com/topics/audio-processing (C++, sorted by recently updated) listing; benchmarks/README.md and results.json read via raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: rkvdec-vdpu383 HEVC/H.264 read-cache fix
baseline: Mainline Linux rkvdec-vdpu383 HEVC and H.264 backends (upstream driver without read-cache configuration); vendor MPP stack as reference
workload: Pure hardware decode time of a 1080p clip on the RK3576 VDPU383 decoder, read cache off versus on, kernel 7.0.1-edge-rockchip64.
claimed_speedup: HEVC about 12 ms to 1.70 ms (~7x, equal to vendor MPP); H.264 8.7 ms to 3.6 ms (~2.4x).
tradeoffs: Kernel patch for Rockchip RK3576 only; module parameter hevc_cache is on by default. README reports a remaining ~1.9x gap to the vendor stack (FBC and one more factor) on all codecs.
caveats: The speedup is a missing cache configuration fixed in an upstream driver, not a new decoder design, and the baseline is a kernel driver rather than FFmpeg, x264 or Opus. First-party numbers on unnamed test streams, no compiler data. README states HEVC output is byte-identical (md5) with the cache on; no H.264 checksum quoted. The commit page shows the commits co-authored with an AI assistant. Very new repo (initial publish 2026-06-28).
found_via: github.com/topics/video-decoder listing flagged 'Performance claims'; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com and commits page opened.
